svg.title: Five ways to stabilise a conjugate base
svg.desc: A banner states the single principle: acidity is set by how well the conjugate base can carry the negative charge left behind, so every structural rule below is a way of spreading or steadying that charge. Five cards follow, each with a worked comparison. Electronegativity, which governs comparisons across a period: methane at about fifty, ammonia at thirty-eight, water at fifteen point seven and hydrogen fluoride at three point two, because the more electronegative atom holds the lone pair more comfortably; across a period, electronegativity wins. Atomic size and bond strength, which governs comparisons down a group: hydrogen fluoride at three point two against hydrogen iodide at about minus ten, a difference of thirteen pKa units, because the H-F bond dissociation energy of about 570 kilojoules per mole against about 297 for H-I matters more than fluorine's electronegativity, and the larger iodide spreads the charge over a far bigger volume; down a group, size wins. Resonance: ethanol at sixteen, phenol at ten and acetic acid at four point seven six, because ethoxide holds the charge on one oxygen, phenoxide spreads it into the ring, and acetate spreads it equally over two equivalent oxygens, which is the strongest case. Induction: acetic acid at four point seven six, fluoroacetic at two point six six, difluoroacetic at one point two four and trifluoroacetic at nought point five two, electron-withdrawing groups pulling charge away through the sigma bonds, additively, and falling off sharply with distance, so chloroacetic acid at two point eight six is far more acidic than 3-chloropropanoic acid at about four point zero. Hybridisation, for carbon-hydrogen bonds: sp3 methane at about fifty with twenty-five per cent s-character, sp2 ethylene at about forty-four with thirty-three per cent, and sp acetylene at about twenty-five with fifty per cent, because more s-character holds the lone pair closer to the nucleus. A footer gives the reaction test: a proton transfer is favourable when the acid formed is weaker than the acid consumed, so compute the pKa of the product acid minus the pKa of the reactant acid and require it to be positive, and K equals ten raised to that difference. Hydroxide and ethanol give fifteen point seven minus sixteen, which is minus nought point three, so very slightly unfavourable and effectively thermoneutral. Hydroxide and acetylene give fifteen point seven minus twenty-five, which is minus nine point three, so hopeless, and you need amide or butyllithium instead.
svg.text: Five ways to stabilise a conjugate base
Acid strength is not about the proton. It is about how comfortably the anion left behind can hold the charge.
One principle underneath all five
Acidity is set by how comfortably the conjugate base can carry the charge left behind. Every rule below is a way of spreading or
steadying that charge.
ELECTRONEGATIVITY
across a period
CH₄ 50 · NH₃ 38 · H₂O 15.7 · HF 3.2
The more electronegative atom holds the lone pair
more comfortably. Across a period, electronegativity
wins.
SIZE & BOND STRENGTH
down a group
HF 3.2 → HI ≈ −10 (Δ ≈ 13 pKₐ units)
H–F bond 570 kJ/mol vs H–I 297; and iodide spreads
the charge over a far larger volume. Down a group,
size wins — not electronegativity.
RESONANCE
how many atoms share the charge
ethanol 16 · phenol 10 · acetic acid 4.76
Ethoxide holds it on one oxygen; phenoxide spreads
it into the ring; acetate splits it equally between
two equivalent oxygens.
INDUCTION
through the sigma bonds — additive, and distance-sensitive
CH₃COOH 4.76 · FCH₂COOH 2.66 · F₂CHCOOH 1.24 · F₃CCOOH 0.52
Each electron-withdrawing group pulls charge away.
The effect falls off fast: chloroacetic 2.86 vs
3-chloropropanoic ≈ 4.0.
HYBRIDISATION
for C–H bonds only
sp³ CH₄ 50 · sp² C₂H₄ 44 · sp C₂H₂ 25
More s-character holds the lone pair closer to the
The reaction test — mind the sign
A proton transfer is favourable when the acid you make is weaker than the acid you consume: ΔpKₐ = pKₐ(product acid) − pKₐ(reactant
acid), favourable when positive, and K = 10^ΔpKₐ. OH⁻ + ethanol: 15.7 − 16 = −0.3, so very slightly unfavourable — effectively
thermoneutral. OH⁻ + acetylene: 15.7 − 25 = −9.3, hopeless; use NaNH₂ or n-BuLi.
